rationale: A wins because it stays closer to what Anker can actually prove and sends the founder to the right next move. Its "The power-bank company just built a whole-home battery" is a real brand-trust angle with honest proof gaps; B's "A profitable public electronics giant is funding its own move into home energy" smuggles in financing logic the update does not give us. B has brains, but it keeps adding little stage props, and those are how pitches become corrections.
gaps_in_A: "Anker naming Tesla Powerwall as direct competition" overstates the update; the facts say Anker competes with Powerwall, not that Anker named Tesla in its launch positioning.

"The power-bank company just built a whole-home battery" and "Why a phone-charger giant is betting on home energy storage" partly overlap on the same identity leap. One needs a sharper protagonist, such as homeowner trust, installer friction, or investor materiality.
"Story type: category-creation" is loose for the third angle. That angle is really corporate diversification or capital-allocation strategy, not proof of a new category.
The set misses a possible homeowner-economics lens, but correctly holds back because pricing, capacity, and savings data are thin.
gaps_in_B: "a brand the public knows for $30 cables" is invented color. The update says phone chargers and power banks, not cable pricing.
"self-funding entry" is not grounded. Large, profitable, and publicly traded does not prove Anker is funding the move internally or carrying the balance-sheet risk alone.
"unlike a venture-backed energy startup" creates a convenient foil not supplied by the facts. It sounds smart, which is exactly why it is dangerous.

"Next step: `newsjack-detector`" is the wrong handoff. This is already pegged to a US launch; the next step is journalist-fit-check plus proof gathering, not wandering off to manufacture an external hook.
